subproblems.title: Near a point of ray(e), the union of the open rays of finitely many unit vectors is contained in ray(e) (parent steps 2–3)
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let F ⊆ ℝ^P be a finite set of unit vectors (‖e'‖ = 1 for every e' ∈ F), let e ∈ ℝ^P be a unit vector (e need not belong to F), and let t₀ > 0. Write ray(w) := {t·w : t > 0}. Then there is δ > 0 such that every point of the open ball B_δ(t₀e) that lies on ray(e') for some e' ∈ F lies on ray(e); that is, B_δ(t₀e) ∩ ⋃_{e'∈F} ray(e') ⊆ ray(e).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (F : Finset (Euclid P)) (e : Euclid P) (t₀ : ℝ), (∀ e' ∈ F, ‖e'‖ = 1) → ‖e‖ = 1 → 0 < t₀ → ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ball (t₀ • e) δ ∩ (⋃ e' ∈ F, (fun t : ℝ => t • e') '' Ioi 0) ⊆ (fun t : ℝ => t • e) '' Ioi 0
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: steps 2–3 of the parent proof of the selected theorem idtp_fons_odc_ray_orientation, i.e. the isolation of ray(e) at x = t₀e and the geometric half of the local inclusion M ∩ B_δ(x) ⊆ (x + L) ∪ N. Here it is extracted for an arbitrary finite set F of unit vectors and an arbitrary unit vector e; membership e ∈ F is not needed.

Notation: x := t₀e; ray(w) := {t·w : t > 0}; for w ∈ ℝ^P, γ_w(s) := s·w (s ∈ ℝ) and C(w) := γ_w([0, ∞)) = {s·w : s ≥ 0}; B_δ(x) is the open ball of radius δ about x.

1. (Closed rays are closed.) Let e' ∈ F. For s, s' ∈ ℝ, ‖γ_{e'}(s) − γ_{e'}(s')‖ = ‖(s − s')·e'‖ = |s − s'|·‖e'‖ = |s − s'|, so γ_{e'} : ℝ → ℝ^P is an isometry. An isometry defined on the complete space ℝ is a closed embedding (Mathlib Isometry.isClosedEmbedding), so it maps the closed set [0, ∞) onto a closed set. Hence C(e') is closed.
2. (The closed rays of the other directions.) Let K := ⋃_{e' ∈ F, e' ≠ e} C(e'). Since F is finite, K is a finite union of closed sets, hence closed.
3. (x ∉ K.) Suppose x ∈ K, i.e. t₀·e = s·e' for some e' ∈ F with e' ≠ e and some s ≥ 0. Take norms, using t₀ > 0, s ≥ 0 and ‖e‖ = ‖e'‖ = 1: t₀ = |t₀|·‖e‖ = ‖t₀·e‖ = ‖s·e'‖ = |s|·‖e'‖ = s. Hence t₀·e = t₀·e'. Multiplying by t₀⁻¹ (t₀ ≠ 0) gives e = e', contradicting e' ≠ e. So x ∉ K.
4. (Choice of δ.) The complement ℝ^P ∖ K is open (step 2) and contains x (step 3), so there is δ > 0 with B_δ(x) ⊆ ℝ^P ∖ K.
5. (Conclusion.) Let y ∈ B_δ(x) ∩ ⋃_{e'∈F} ray(e'). Then y = t·e'' for some e'' ∈ F and some t > 0. If e'' ≠ e, then, since t ≥ 0, y ∈ C(e'') ⊆ K, contradicting y ∈ B_δ(x) ⊆ ℝ^P ∖ K. Hence e'' = e and y = t·e with t > 0, i.e. y ∈ ray(e). Thus this δ > 0 satisfies B_δ(t₀e) ∩ ⋃_{e'∈F} ray(e') ⊆ ray(e). ∎
proof_key_steps: For each e' ∈ F, s ↦ s·e' is an isometry of ℝ into ℝ^P, so the closed ray {s·e' : s ≥ 0} is closed, and K := ⋃_{e'∈F, e'≠e} {s·e' : s ≥ 0} is closed.
t₀e ∉ K: t₀·e = s·e' with s ≥ 0 forces s = t₀ by comparing norms, and then e' = e.
Openness of ℝ^P ∖ K gives δ > 0 with B_δ(t₀e) ∩ K = ∅.
A point t·e'' (t > 0, e'' ∈ F) of that ball cannot have e'' ≠ e, so it lies on ray(e).

subproblems.title: A nonnegative continuous compactly supported function that is positive at a unit vector u has positive H¹-integral over the line ℝu (parent step 4a)
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let u ∈ ℝ^P with ‖u‖ = 1, and let f : ℝ^P → ℝ be continuous with compact support, f(y) ≥ 0 for all y, and f(u) > 0. Then ∫_{span{u}} f dH¹ > 0, where H¹ = μHE[1] is the normalized 1-dimensional Hausdorff measure on ℝ^P and the integral is taken over the line span{u} = ℝu (with respect to H¹ restricted to that set).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (u : Euclid P) (f : Euclid P → ℝ), ‖u‖ = 1 → Continuous f → HasCompactSupport f → (∀ y, 0 ≤ f y) → 0 < f u → 0 < ∫ y in (Submodule.span ℝ {u} : Set (Euclid P)), f y ∂(μHE[1] : Measure (Euclid P))
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 4a of the parent proof of the selected theorem idtp_fons_odc_ray_orientation (“∫_Q f dH¹ > 0: by line_param (p = 0, v = u, I = ℝ), H¹⌞Q = (t ↦ tu)_#ℒ¹ …”), stated here for an arbitrary nonnegative continuous compactly supported f.

It uses the selected node's prerequisite line_param, Lean name Submission.idtp_fons_odc_line_hausdorff, whose frozen type is: unitBallVolume 1 = 2 ∧ ∀ (P : ℕ) (p v : Euclid P), ‖v‖ = 1 → MeasurableEmbedding (fun t : ℝ => p + t • v) ∧ ∀ I : Set ℝ, (μHE[1] : Measure (Euclid P)).restrict ((fun t : ℝ => p + t • v) '' I) = Measure.map (fun t : ℝ => p + t • v) (volume.restrict I) ∧ (μHE[1] : Measure (Euclid P)) ((fun t : ℝ => p + t • v) '' I) = volume I.

Notation: γ(t) := 0 + t·u = t·u for t ∈ ℝ; ℒ¹ := volume on ℝ; H¹ := μHE[1] on ℝ^P.

1. (line_param.) Apply the second conjunct of Submission.idtp_fons_odc_line_hausdorff to this P, p = 0 and v = u (‖u‖ = 1). It says that γ is a measurable embedding ℝ → ℝ^P. Taking I = ℝ (Set.univ), it also says H¹⌞γ(ℝ) = γ_#(ℒ¹⌞ℝ) = γ_#ℒ¹, since ℒ¹ restricted to all of ℝ is ℒ¹.
2. (The line is γ(ℝ).) y ∈ span{u} iff y = a·u for some a ∈ ℝ, and a·u = γ(a). Hence span{u} = γ(ℝ) as sets.
3. (Change of variables.) By steps 1–2, ∫_{span{u}} f dH¹ = ∫ f d(H¹⌞γ(ℝ)) = ∫ f d(γ_#ℒ¹) = ∫_ℝ f(γ(t)) dt. The last equality is the integral formula for the push-forward of a measure under a measurable embedding (Mathlib MeasurableEmbedding.integral_map), which needs no integrability hypothesis.
4. (Properties of g := f ∘ γ.) g(t) = f(t·u) is continuous, as a composition of continuous maps, and g ≥ 0 everywhere. γ is an isometry, because ‖γ(s) − γ(t)‖ = |s − t|·‖u‖ = |s − t|, hence a closed embedding of ℝ into ℝ^P. The support of g is contained in γ⁻¹(spt f), which is compact because spt f is compact and preimages of compact sets under a closed embedding are compact. So g has compact support (Mathlib HasCompactSupport.comp_isClosedEmbedding). Finally g(1) = f(1·u) = f(u) > 0.
5. (Positivity on ℝ.) g is integrable, being continuous with compact support while ℒ¹ is finite on compact sets. By continuity there is an open interval J ∋ 1 of positive length on which g > g(1)/2. Since g ≥ 0, ∫_ℝ g dt ≥ (g(1)/2)·ℒ¹(J) > 0 (Mathlib Continuous.integral_pos_of_hasCompactSupport_nonneg_nonzero, at the point 1).
6. By step 3, ∫_{span{u}} f dH¹ = ∫_ℝ g dt > 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: Submission.idtp_fons_odc_line_hausdorff with p = 0, v = u, I = ℝ: t ↦ t·u is a measurable embedding and H¹⌞(ℝu) = (t ↦ t·u)_#ℒ¹.
span{u} is the image of t ↦ t·u, so ∫_{span{u}} f dH¹ = ∫_ℝ f(t·u) dt by the push-forward formula for measurable embeddings.
t ↦ f(t·u) is continuous, nonnegative, compactly supported (t ↦ t·u is an isometric closed embedding) and positive at t = 1, so its Lebesgue integral is positive.

subproblems.title: If M lies near x in the line x + ℝv up to an H¹-null set, every 1-dimensional approximate tangent space of M at x is ℝv (parent step 4)
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (M N : Set (Euclid P)) (x v : Euclid P) (δ : ℝ) (Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), v ≠ 0 → 0 < δ → (μHE[1] : Measure (Euclid P)) N = 0 → M ∩ ball x δ ⊆ range (fun s : ℝ => x + s • v) ∪ N → HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 1 M x Q → Q = Submodule.span ℝ {v}
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 4 of the parent proof of the selected theorem idtp_fons_odc_ray_orientation (“The approximate tangent line at x is L”). It is extracted here for an arbitrary set M, an arbitrary H¹-null set N and an arbitrary nonzero direction v, with the line written as {x + s·v : s ∈ ℝ}. In the parent it is applied with x = t₀e, v = e and N = R.carrier ∖ ⋃_{e'∈F} ray(e'). Step 4a of the parent is the sibling line_integral_pos (Lean name Submission.idtp_fons_odc_ro_line_integral_pos).

Notation: H¹ := μHE[1]; L := span{v} = {a·v : a ∈ ℝ}; ℓ := {x + s·v : s ∈ ℝ}; η_r := blowUpMap x r, so η_r(y) = r⁻¹(y − x); B_δ(x) is the open ball.

1. (Three elementary facts.)
 (a) For r ≠ 0 and any S ⊆ ℝ^P: η_r(S) = {y : x + r·y ∈ S}, because y = r⁻¹(z − x) iff z = x + r·y.
 (b) For r > 0, η_r is Lipschitz with constant |r⁻¹|, since ‖η_r(a) − η_r(b)‖ = |r⁻¹|·‖a − b‖. By the Lipschitz image bound for the normalized Hausdorff measure (SimonGMT Chapter02 euclideanHausdorffMeasure_image_le_of_lipschitzOn with n = 1), H¹(η_r(N)) ≤ |r⁻¹|·H¹(N) = 0.
 (c) For ρ ≠ 0 and y ∈ ℝ^P: x + ρ·y ∈ ℓ iff y ∈ L. If x + ρ·y = x + s·v, then y = (ρ⁻¹s)·v ∈ L. If y = a·v, then x + ρ·y = x + (ρa)·v ∈ ℓ.
2. (Reduction.) finrank Q = 1 by the first component of HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 1 M x Q, and finrank L = 1 because v ≠ 0. A subspace contained in a finite-dimensional subspace of the same dimension equals it (Submodule.eq_of_le_of_finrank_eq). So it suffices to prove Q ≤ L. Suppose, for a contradiction, that Q ⊄ L.
3. (A unit vector u ∈ Q ∖ L.) Choose w ∈ Q with w ∉ L; w ≠ 0 because 0 ∈ L. Put u := ‖w‖⁻¹·w. Then u ∈ Q, ‖u‖ = 1, and u ∉ L (otherwise w = ‖w‖·u ∈ L). Since u ≠ 0, span{u} is a 1-dimensional subspace of Q, and finrank Q = 1, so span{u} = Q.
4. (The bump function.) Let d := dist(u, L) = inf_{a∈ℝ} ‖u − a·v‖. L is finite-dimensional, hence closed, and nonempty, and u ∉ L, so d > 0. Define f(y) := max(0, d/2 − ‖y − u‖). f is continuous and f ≥ 0. Also f(y) = 0 whenever ‖y − u‖ > d/2, so f vanishes outside the compact closed ball B̄(u, d/2) and has compact support. Thus f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P, ℝ), and f(u) = max(0, d/2) = d/2 > 0.
5. (The limit is positive.) Apply the sibling line_integral_pos (Submission.idtp_fons_odc_ro_line_integral_pos) to u (‖u‖ = 1) and f (continuous, compactly supported, f ≥ 0, f(u) > 0). It gives ∫_{span{u}} f dH¹ > 0, which by step 3 says ∫_Q f dH¹ > 0.
6. (The blown-up integrals vanish.) Let 0 < ρ < δ/(1 + d); the bound is positive since δ > 0 and d > 0, and ρ(1 + d) < δ.
 Claim: every y ∈ η_ρ(M) with f(y) ≠ 0 lies in η_ρ(N). By 1(a), z := x + ρ·y ∈ M. As f(y) ≠ 0, ‖y − u‖ < d/2 (if ‖y − u‖ ≥ d/2 then d/2 − ‖y − u‖ ≤ 0 and f(y) = 0). Hence ‖y‖ ≤ ‖u‖ + ‖y − u‖ < 1 + d/2 < 1 + d, and ‖z − x‖ = ρ·‖y‖ < ρ(1 + d) < δ. So z ∈ M ∩ B_δ(x) ⊆ ℓ ∪ N. If z ∈ ℓ, then y ∈ L by 1(c), whence d = dist(u, L) ≤ ‖u − y‖ < d/2, impossible because d > 0. Therefore z = x + ρ·y ∈ N, i.e. y ∈ η_ρ(N) by 1(a).
 By 1(b), η_ρ(N) is H¹-null, so f(y) = 0 for H¹-almost every y ∈ η_ρ(M). Hence ∫_{η_ρ(M)} f dH¹ = 0, because an integrand vanishing almost everywhere on the domain of integration has integral 0 (Mathlib setIntegral_eq_zero_of_ae_eq_zero; this needs no measurability of η_ρ(M), M or N).
7. (Contradiction.) By step 6, the function r ↦ ∫_{η_r(M)} f dH¹ is 0 on (0, δ/(1 + d)), which belongs to the right-neighbourhood filter 𝓝[>] 0; so it tends to 0 as r ↓ 0. By the second component of HasApproximateTangentSpaceAt 1 M x Q, applied to f ∈ C_c(ℝ^P, ℝ), the same function tends to ∫_Q f dH¹ as r ↓ 0. Limits in ℝ along the non-trivial filter 𝓝[>] 0 are unique, so ∫_Q f dH¹ = 0, contradicting step 5. Hence Q ≤ L, and by step 2, Q = L = span{v}. ∎
proof_key_steps: η_{x,r}(S) = {y : x + r·y ∈ S} for r ≠ 0; η_{x,r} is |r⁻¹|-Lipschitz, so η_{x,r}(N) is H¹-null; x + ρ·y lies on x + ℝv iff y ∈ ℝv.
Since finrank Q = 1 = finrank ℝv, it suffices to rule out Q ⊄ ℝv. In that case pick a unit u ∈ Q ∖ ℝv; then Q = ℝu and d = dist(u, ℝv) > 0.
For f(y) = max(0, d/2 − ‖y − u‖) ∈ C_c, line_integral_pos gives ∫_Q f dH¹ > 0.
For 0 < ρ < δ/(1+d), every y ∈ η_{x,ρ}(M) with f(y) ≠ 0 has x + ρ·y ∈ B_δ(x) and off the line, hence in N. So ∫_{η_{x,ρ}(M)} f dH¹ = 0.
Uniqueness of limits as r ↓ 0 forces ∫_Q f dH¹ = 0, a contradiction; hence Q = ℝv.

subproblems.title: A unit orientation of the line ℝe (‖e‖ = 1) is ±(α ↦ α(e)) (parent step 5)
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let e ∈ ℝ^P with ‖e‖ = 1, and let ξ ∈ Λ_1(ℝ^P) (MultiVector P 1, the continuous linear functionals on 1-covectors) satisfy IsUnitOrientationOf ξ (span{e}). That is, there is an orthonormal τ : Fin 1 → ℝ^P with span(range τ) = span{e} such that either ξ(α) = α(τ) for all 1-covectors α, or ξ(α) = −α(τ) for all α. Then ξ = ev_e or ξ = −ev_e, where ev_e = ContinuousAlternatingMap.apply ℝ (Euclid P) ℝ (fun _ : Fin 1 => e) is the 1-vector α ↦ α(fun _ => e).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (e : Euclid P) (ξ : MultiVector P 1), ‖e‖ = 1 → IsUnitOrientationOf ξ (Submodule.span ℝ {e}) → ξ = ContinuousAlternatingMap.apply ℝ (Euclid P) ℝ (fun _ : Fin 1 => e) ∨ ξ = -ContinuousAlternatingMap.apply ℝ (Euclid P) ℝ (fun _ : Fin 1 => e)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 5 of the parent proof of the selected theorem idtp_fons_odc_ray_orientation (“Unit orientations of L”), stated here for an arbitrary unit vector e and an arbitrary unit orientation ξ of span{e}.

Notation: a 1-covector α is a continuous alternating map (ℝ^P)^{Fin 1} → ℝ. For w ∈ ℝ^P, α[w] := α(fun _ => w). ev_e := ContinuousAlternatingMap.apply ℝ (Euclid P) ℝ (fun _ : Fin 1 => e), so ev_e(α) = α[e] (ContinuousAlternatingMap.apply_apply).

1. (Unpacking.) By IsUnitOrientationOf ξ (span{e}) there is an orthonormal τ : Fin 1 → ℝ^P with span(range τ) = span{e} such that either (A) ξ(α) = α(τ) for all 1-covectors α, or (B) ξ(α) = −α(τ) for all α.
2. (τ 0 is a multiple of e.) τ 0 ∈ range τ ⊆ span(range τ) = span{e}, so τ 0 = c·e for some c ∈ ℝ (Submodule.mem_span_singleton).
3. (c = ±1.) Orthonormality gives ‖τ 0‖ = 1, so 1 = ‖c·e‖ = |c|·‖e‖ = |c|. Hence c = 1 or c = −1.
4. (Evaluation.) Fin 1 has exactly one element, 0, so τ = (fun _ => c·e). α is multilinear in its single argument: α(fun i => c_i·m_i) = (∏_i c_i)·α(m) (ContinuousAlternatingMap.map_smul_univ, here with the single factor c). Hence α(τ) = α(fun _ => c·e) = c·α[e] for every 1-covector α.
5. (Four sign cases.) Two continuous linear maps on the space of 1-covectors are equal once they agree at every α.
 - (A) with c = 1: ξ(α) = α[e] = ev_e(α) for all α, so ξ = ev_e.
 - (A) with c = −1: ξ(α) = −α[e] = (−ev_e)(α), so ξ = −ev_e.
 - (B) with c = 1: ξ(α) = −α[e], so ξ = −ev_e.
 - (B) with c = −1: ξ(α) = −(−α[e]) = α[e], so ξ = ev_e.
 In every case ξ = ev_e or ξ = −ev_e. ∎
proof_key_steps: Unpack IsUnitOrientationOf: an orthonormal τ : Fin 1 → ℝ^P with span(range τ) = ℝe and ξ = ±(α ↦ α(τ)).
τ 0 ∈ ℝe and ‖τ 0‖ = 1 = ‖e‖ give τ 0 = c·e with c = ±1.
τ = (fun _ => c·e), so α(τ) = c·α(e) by multilinearity, and the four sign cases give ξ = ±ev_e by extensionality.
